paras: The attempted lynching of John Dickson took place in Longview, Texas, in August 1900, when local citizens planned to take Dickson, a Black man charged with attempted assault on a white girl, from jail and hang him. Sheriff Howard moved the prisoner out of town before the mob arrived, and Texas papers reported the episode as a lynching foiled by the sheriff.

According to a Longview dispatch dated August 15, on the morning of the 14th a Black man entered the home of Mrs. J. W. Joplin, a widow, and tried to assault and choke her 15-year-old daughter. He ran off when the girl cried out, and her mother fired at him three times; the girl was said to have identified him.

That night Sheriff Howard "got wind that the best citizens of the community were going to take the negro out of jail and hang him." About dusk he took "the best team in town" and drove the prisoner away. When the lynching "committee" reached the jail around 10:30 p.m., it found him gone.

The crowd was "very indignant at the prompt action taken by the sheriff." The Houston dispatch placed the prisoner in Marshall or Gilmer; the El Paso Daily Herald later named him John Dickson and put him in the county jail at Marshall. No report of a trial or later outcome was found.

Only white Texas papers carried the story; no Black-press report was found. The Houston Daily Post of August 17 put it in its front-page news summary and ran the dispatch on page 8 as "Attempted Assault. Negro Identified by Girl—Lynching Party Disappointed." The Post stated the accusation as fact, called the would-be lynchers "the best citizens" and "the committee," and said of the escape that "the bird had flown."

The El Paso Daily Herald's brief of August 23, headed "Sheriff Foils a Mob," ran in a column of Texas news. It credited the sheriff and called the would-be lynchers "a mob of enraged citizens," while describing Dickson only as "a negro charged with attempted assault on a young white girl."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Dickson
bases: A party of citizens went to the Longview jail at night intending to take an accused Black prisoner out and hang him, but the sheriff had already removed him (A2, A3).

The papers describe a planned lynching by a 'mob' or 'committee' of citizens acting on an accusation of attempted assault, but the sheriff removed the prisoner beforehand and no one was killed (A2, A3); it was a threatened or attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Houston Post's Longview dispatch (A2) and the El Paso Herald's brief (A3) agree on the accusation, the planned lynching and the sheriff's removal of the prisoner; A3 adds the name and destination not in A2, so it was not copied from A2, though both may go back to the same Texas news report.

accounts.label: Longview dispatch
accounts.gist: A Black man entered the Joplin home on the 14th and tried to choke and assault the daughter; the sheriff, hearing the 'best citizens' planned to hang the prisoner, removed him at dusk, and the committee found the jail empty about 10:30 p.m.

accounts.label: Texas news column
accounts.gist: A mob of enraged citizens at Longview organized to lynch John Dickson, charged with attempted assault on a young white girl; Sheriff Howard learned of it and had him moved to the county jail at Marshall.

framing.detail: The Houston Post headed its dispatch 'ATTEMPTED ASSAULT. Negro Identified by Girl—Lynching Party Disappointed,' stated the accusation as fact, called the lynchers 'the best citizens' and 'the committee', and treated the escape lightly ('the bird had flown').
The El Paso Herald's 'Sheriff Foils a Mob' credited the sheriff and called the would-be lynchers a 'mob of enraged citizens.'

conflicts.note: The local dispatch was uncertain; the later El Paso brief names Marshall only. Not a direct contradiction.
